title: Scientists Finally Recreate a 1,600-Year-Old Color-Changing Cup
summary: About 1,600 years ago, Roman glassmakers created a cup that changes colour like magic. Now, scientists have finally figured out how to make it again. The Lycurgus Cup, now on display at the British Museum, is one of the most famous pieces of Roman glass in the world. It is one of only 40 surviving glass cage cups. Look at it in reflected light and it appears jade green. Shine a light through it and it glows ruby red. Glassmakers have long wondered how the Romans pulled off this trick, called the dichroic effect. The leading explanation is that Roman craftspeople mixed tiny amounts of gold and silver into the glass. These metals form particles thousands of times smaller than a grain of sand, called nanoparticles. Because the particles are smaller than the wavelengths of light, they absorb and scatter certain colours depending on their size and shape. Lisa Hollands, a team leader at the University of Sheffield who has worked with glass for more than 25 years, set out to crack the recipe with Caroline Jackson, a leading expert on Roman glass. She tried different furnace types, starting materials with different oxygen levels, and even sugar. At last, she found a recipe that works: her glass looks opaque green in reflected light and glows red when light shines through. Hollands explained that the particles block blue and green light when light shines through, letting only reds and oranges pass. The team asked glass artist Elliot Walker, who won season two of Netflix's "Blown Away," to use the recipe in a new sculpture. The sculpture goes on display at the university's Festival of the Mind on November 6, before moving permanently into the school's Turner Museum of Glass. The science could go further than art: it may lead to new materials that control light, and to advanced glasses for safely storing radioactive waste.
why_it_matters: Ancient crafts can teach modern science new tricks, and this one may help build materials that control light or store waste safely.

Radioactive means giving off energy from atoms breaking apart.
